subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: attempting first, then asking for feedback [Action]
passage: Teacher's note, Shalini. Ankit brought his essay draft on Tuesday with a page of comments in the margin. He had written the whole first draft himself, then asked an AI tool two questions: which parts were unclear, and how the structure could be tighter. He did not paste in any of its sentences. The tool said his second paragraph jumped between two ideas, so he split it and rewrote both halves in his own words. He showed me both versions. The second draft was clearer, and, more importantly, he could explain why. I asked how he decided what to keep from the feedback, and he said he kept whatever made sense to him. I have told him that this order, own thinking first and feedback second, is a good habit for other subjects too.

qa.q: Which two questions did Ankit ask the tool?
qa.a: Ankit asked which parts were unclear and how the structure could be tighter.

qa.q: What might Ankit feel when he explains why the second draft is clearer?
qa.a: Ankit probably feels proud and confident, since he understands the changes as his own.

qa.q: What could Ankit do if the tool's feedback is confusing?
qa.a: Ankit could check with Shalini or a classmate, since a person who knows the assignment can say which comments to keep.

qa.q: How might Shalini see this way of working?
qa.a: Shalini sees own thinking first and feedback second as a good habit, and wants to encourage it in other subjects.

grounding: A student writes his own essay draft, then asks an AI what is unclear and how to improve the structure, and rewrites the text himself.
